title: [Chapitre] II. Réalisations topologiques des réseaux : notes manuscrites (06/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. A 'ficelle' (string) is a pair F=(X,{A,B}): a space X with two distinguished closed 'ends' A and B. A 'lien' (link, or cut) of F is a closed subset C that cuts X into an A-side and a B-side meeting exactly along C. Page 6 gives the criterion for this in terms of local connectedness at C. In the proof, after collapsing A, B, C, D to points a, b, c, d, the condition reads X = X_{a,c} ⊔_c X_{c,b}: X is a pushout, i.e. two bipointed pieces glued along the single point c.

Cutting. Cutting F at an interior link C (C not equal to A or B) gives two strings, F_{A,C}=(X_{A,C},{A,C}) and F_{B,C}=(X_{C,B},{C,B}). Every link of either piece is a link of F.

Categorical reformulation (two items). Grothendieck plans an equivalence of categories, which the next page states explicitly in the oriented case. On one side: (a) strings with a chosen interior link. On the other: (b) pairs of strings together with a homeomorphism between an end of one and an end of the other. Cutting goes from (a) to (b); gluing along the homeomorphism goes from (b) to (a). This is concatenation of 'bipointed' objects.

Lemma. Let C and D be distinct interior links of F. Then D is a link of F_{B,C} if and only if C is a link of F_{A,D}. Swapping A with B and C with D gives the symmetric form: D is a link of F_{A,C} iff C is a link of F_{B,D}. The margin picture 'A C D B' is the order intuition behind this.

Proof. It suffices to prove one direction; the other follows by the swap. One may assume ('OPS' = on peut supposer) that A, B, C, D are points. Since c is a link, X = X_{a,c} ⊔_c X_{c,b}. Since d is a link of X_{c,b}, X_{c,b} = X_{c,d} ⊔_d X_{d,b}. By associativity of the pushout, X = (X_{a,c} ⊔_c X_{c,d}) ⊔_d X_{d,b}. So the A-side of d is X_{a,d} = X_{a,c} ⊔_c X_{c,d}, and c is visibly a link of it.

Purpose. This prepares the 'disjointness' relation of page 8: two interior links C≠D are disjoint iff D is a link of F_{A,C} or of F_{B,C}. It also prepares the order C ≤ D on the links of an oriented string. The aim is to show that the links of a string form a linearly ordered, interval-like structure. This underlies the topological realisation of networks (graphs) by gluing strings at their ends.
errors: The proof is a sketch. It implicitly uses the following facts. (1) The decomposition of X at a link is uniquely determined by the link, so the X_{a,d} built by associativity is the X_{a,d} attached to d as a link of F. (2) d, being a link of F_{B,C}, is a link of F; this is the preceding claim that links of components are links of F. (3) Collapsing A, B, C, D to points is harmless. Point (3) needs the ends and links to be compact or at least closed with a well-behaved quotient. None of these is justified on the page, but all are plausible within his definitions.
The '⇐ follows by swapping' step is correct only when the swap is done exactly as stated: A↔B and C↔D together. Doing so turns the statement into its converse.

ideas.what: Strings (ficelles) as spaces with two ends, cut at 'links' into two strings; the category of strings with an interior link is equivalent to pairs of strings with an end-to-end identification
ideas.modern_name: Concatenation/juxtaposition of bipointed spaces; composition of 1-dimensional cobordisms; pushouts of bipointed objects
ideas.usually_credited_to: Freyd (bipointed sets/juxtaposition, characterisation of [0,1], ~1999); Leinster (general theory of self-similarity, 2011); cobordism categories more generally

ideas.what: Lemma: for interior links C≠D, D is a link of F_{B,C} iff C is a link of F_{A,D} (betweenness/order of cuts), proved by associativity of gluing
ideas.modern_name: Separation order of cut points / cut sets in continuum theory (betweenness relation on cut points of arcs, dendrites)
ideas.usually_credited_to: R.L. Moore, Kuratowski, G.T. Whyburn, L.E. Ward (cutpoint order), early-to-mid 20th century

missed.claim: Grothendieck's ficelles are bipointed spaces glued end-to-end by pushouts, with a category of 'strings with an interior cut' equivalent to composable pairs. This is essentially the juxtaposition structure Freyd later used to characterise [0,1] as a terminal coalgebra, and that Leinster generalised to self-similar spaces. The 1986 manuscript seems to anticipate this framework in a topological rather than coalgebraic setting.
missed.quote: b) Paires de ficelles, avec homéo entre un bout de l'une, un bout de l'autre.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical note only. Grothendieck's intrinsic 'string' axiomatics (links, orders of cuts) could be compared with Freyd–Leinster's coalgebraic characterisation of the interval, and with his own later 'réseaux' realisations. The content itself is elementary.

deep.surprise_reason: Elementary, correct point-set lemma on the order of cuts in a string-like space, proved by associativity of pushouts. It is part of an unpublished but routine foundational setup. The only mildly interesting aspect is the categorical concatenation viewpoint, which resembles later Freyd/Leinster work.
transcription_corrections: 'Épreuve[?] de Catégories[?]' should be 'Équivalence de catégories'. The next page continues 'est équivalente', and the a)/b) list describes the two sides of an equivalence.
'lieu'/'Lieu' throughout is very likely 'lien' (link), matching page 6's heading 'Liens disjoints'. Page 8 switches to 'Lignes'.
'(|| déf X_{b,c})' means that X_{c,b} is by definition the same as X_{b,c}. Likewise '|| déf X_{b,d}'.
Lemma line: read roughly 'Soient C et D deux liens (C≠D) de F, distincts des extrémités'.
